title: A Inheritance for the Parish
premise: When the coffin of Aldous Wren, founder of the river town of Bellhaven, is found empty during a parish exhumation, insurance investigator Marguerite Sterling is pulled into a case that predates every policy he's ever read. Using his photographic memory of a decades-old estate file, Marguerite discovers that Wren's 'inheritance' was never money but a confession naming who really killed his business partner in 1961—and that someone in town has been quietly eliminating everyone who might have read it. As Marguerite closes in on the killer, he realizes the empty coffin was bait meant to draw out the last living witness: himself, as the child who once copied that file. In the end, Marguerite chooses justice outside the law, letting the town bury its myth while slipping the true confession to the partner's descendants—and walking away from the case he finally couldn't close.
about_author: Dominic Okafor is a former claims adjuster from coastal Georgia who spent eleven years reading other people's disasters before turning them into fiction. He writes mysteries about paper trails, small towns, and the debts families refuse to name.

chapters.title: The Exhumation
chapters.summary: Third-person limited on Marguerite Sterling. On a gray morning, the parish exhumes founder Aldous Wren for a cemetery relocation, and the coffin comes up empty except for a 1961 insurance ledger. Marguerite, attending out of professional habit, recognizes the ledger's stamp instantly. The beat is quiet dread—the moment an ordinary job becomes personal.

chapters.title: Photographic
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. He recalls, frame by frame, the estate file he catalogued as a teenage archive clerk: Wren's death benefits, a missing rider, and a page torn out. His boss wants the anomaly handled quietly; the town wants a miracle or a scandal. The emotional beat is Marguerite's pride curdling into unease—his perfect memory has made him a witness.

chapters.title: Bellhaven Remembers Wrong
chapters.summary: Marguerite interviews the town historian, Effie Marsh, whose oral history of Wren contradicts the official record at every turn. She mentions a business partner, Cyrus Bell, who 'moved away' in 1961—though no one can say where. The beat is the first crack in the town's beloved founding myth.

chapters.title: The Torn Page
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Reconstructing the missing page from memory, he finds a beneficiary clause naming Cyrus Bell's daughter, payable upon 'disclosure.' Someone else has clearly been searching: the county archive copy is gone, checked out under a dead man's name. The beat is the shift from mystery to hunt.

chapters.title: The First Accident
chapters.summary: Effie Marsh falls from her library ladder days after their interview. The sheriff calls it carelessness; Marguerite's memory flags that the ladder's lock was new and unbroken. POV alternates to Effie's niece, Ruthie, grieving and suspicious. The beat is fear arriving in a town that trusts itself.

chapters.title: Case File 61-114
chapters.summary: Marguerite returns to his old employer's cold storage and pulls the original file, committing every page to memory before it can vanish. He finds marginalia in Wren's hand—a list of initials, one circled. The beat is exhilaration shadowed by the realization that whoever erased the copies doesn't know what's inside his head.

chapters.title: The Descendants
chapters.summary: Ruthie's POV. Ruthie reveals her grandmother was Cyrus Bell's daughter, died waiting on an inheritance that never came, and left Ruthie a sealed letter she's never dared open. Marguerite asks to see it; she refuses. The beat is two guarded people recognizing they need each other.

chapters.title: What the Ledger Says
chapters.summary: Marguerite decodes the ledger found in the coffin: premium payments on Wren's life continued eleven years past his death—someone was paying to keep a policy alive, and a body in the ground. The empty coffin stops being sacrilege and becomes evidence. The beat is vertigo: the founder may never have been buried at all.

chapters.title: Sheriff Dane
chapters.summary: Marguerite tests Sheriff Dane with a fabricated detail about the exhumation; Dane repeats it back wrong, then warns him off the case with unusual heat. Marguerite can't tell if Dane is corrupt, scared, or protecting someone. The beat is isolation—the law itself now reads as a suspect.

chapters.title: The Circled Initials
chapters.summary: Marguerite matches Wren's initials list to four founding families still prominent in Bellhaven. Three of the four have recently sold land cheap, settled lawsuits fast, or left town abruptly. The fourth family's matriarch, Vivian Ashcombe, invites him to tea. The beat is the hunter realizing he's also being mapped.

chapters.title: Tea with Vivian
chapters.summary: Vivian's POV. Charming and razor-sharp, she dissects Marguerite's investigation over tea and offers him a consulting fee to 'find closure for the parish.' He notices her hands shake only when he mentions 1961. The beat is a duel conducted entirely in courtesy.

chapters.title: Ruthie's Letter
chapters.summary: After a break-in trashes Ruthie's grandmother's house—searchers after the letter, not valuables—Ruthie finally opens it. It names Wren alive in hiding and accuses 'the circle' of killing Cyrus. The beat is grief becoming resolve; Ruthie joins the hunt as an equal.

chapters.title: The Man in the Photographs
chapters.summary: Marguerite cross-references funeral photos from 1972 and finds a gravedigger's face matching young Aldous Wren—alive, present, unremarkable. Wren faked his death and lived among the people who thought they'd killed him. The beat is awe tipping into horror: the victim was the trap-setter.

chapters.title: Midnight in the Archive
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Returning for a final document, he's attacked by someone who quotes Case File 61-114 verbatim—page numbers, clause numbers—and escapes with only a torn glove. The killer knows the file better than he does, which means they've read it more recently than 1961. The beat is Marguerite's confidence shattering.

chapters.title: Who Read It Last
chapters.summary: Ruthie and Marguerite build a timeline of every person with archive access since the file's creation. The list collapses to two names: a long-dead clerk, and the clerk's protégé—Sheriff Dane. The beat is reluctant certainty; the lawman isn't covering up the crime, he's finishing it.

chapters.title: Dane's Confession, Part One
chapters.summary: Dane's POV. Cornered by implication but not proof, Dane recounts how his mentor showed him the file as a boy, how the founding families paid his way through the academy, and how the debt compounded yearly. He insists he's not the killer—but he knows who is. The beat is sympathy for a compromised man.

chapters.title: The Grave That Wasn't
chapters.summary: Following ledger payments to a rural plot, Marguerite and Ruthie dig at an abandoned homestead and find Cyrus Bell's remains—with Wren's ring on the hand. Wren didn't flee; he traded places with the dead man and spent fifty years building the case that would destroy the circle. The beat is grim vindication.

chapters.title: Closure for the Parish
chapters.summary: Vivian Ashcombe hosts the town's Founder's Day gala, where the relocated Wren monument will be unveiled. Marguerite realizes the ceremony is the deadline: the last person who could authenticate the confession—himself—will be publicly, permanently silenced there. The beat is the clock starting to run out loud.

chapters.title: The Unveiling
chapters.summary: At the gala, Marguerite springs his trap: he announces from the stage that the coffin held a ledger, forcing the killer to move before witnesses. In the monument's shadow, Dane turns his gun not on Marguerite but on Vivian's son—the second reader of the file, protecting his father's debt. The beat is chaos breaking the town's composure open.

chapters.title: Ashes and Testimony
chapters.summary: Climax. Vivian's son takes Ruthie hostage in the crypt beneath the monument; Marguerite trades himself, reciting the entire file from memory aloud so the gathered town hears the 1961 murder confessed in full. Dane makes his choice and arrests his own patron's son. The beat is truth spoken in a public square, justice arriving sideways.

chapters.title: What the Law Can't Bury
chapters.summary: Fallout. The courts will take years and may convict no one; the founding families close ranks. Marguerite bypasses them, giving Ruthie the authenticated confession and Bell's remains for a proper burial, letting the parish keep its statue and lose its soul privately. The beat is bittersweet compromise—justice delivered outside the verdict.

chapters.title: An Open File
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV, weeks later. He declines the town's gratitude, files a report that says only 'closed—unresolved,' and leaves Bellhaven by the river road. In his pocket is a photograph Ruthie gave him: young Wren smiling, free. The beat is quiet release—he finally took a case he couldn't close, and it closed him instead.
